title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
summary: How to turn a number of users into requests per second, storage and concurrent requests, with round numbers.

blocks.p: The right design for 100 requests a second is different from the right design for 100,000. One database handles the first. The second needs caches, many servers and a plan for splitting data.
So before you design anything, you estimate. The goal is the right order of magnitude, not a precise answer. An estimate that is within a factor of 10 already rules out most wrong designs.
Rounding a day to 100,000 seconds makes the arithmetic easy and errs on the low side by 14%. That is well inside the margin of any estimate.
Start from daily active users. Multiply by the actions each user takes in a day. Divide by the seconds in a day to get the average rate.

Traffic is not flat. More people use a service in the evening than at 4 am. Multiply the average by a **peak factor** to size for the busiest hour. A factor of 2 to 3 is a common starting assumption. Replace it with real data once you have some.

blocks.caption: From daily users to peak requests per second. Move the sliders to see which input matters most.

blocks.p: Multiply the number of new items a day by their size, then by the days you keep them. Then multiply by the number of copies. Databases and object stores keep several copies of each item so that one failed disk doesn't lose data.

blocks.caption: Storage for uploaded photos over several years, with 3 copies of each photo.

blocks.p: Servers are limited by how many requests they handle at the same time, not only by the rate. **Little's law** connects the two: the average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each one spends there.

At 2,000 requests a second and 200 ms per request, about 400 requests are in progress at any moment. [Little's 1961 paper](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383) proved that this holds for any queue in a steady state, whatever the pattern of arrivals.

list: **Write your assumptions down.** Each input is a guess. Writing it down lets someone else challenge the guess instead of the arithmetic.
**Look for the biggest number.** Usually one quantity dominates: reads far outnumber writes, or video dwarfs everything else in storage. Design around that one.

**Check against the latency numbers.** Say each request reads 1 MB from a spinning disk, and you need 1,000 requests a second. The latency lesson puts 1 MB from disk at 30 ms, so one disk manages about 33.

**Jeff Dean recommends it.** His [2009 talk](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/ladis2009/talks/dean-keynote-ladis2009.pdf) presents back-of-the-envelope calculations as a core design skill, alongside the latency numbers.

blocks.p: Size a photo sharing app. Set the users, how many photos they view and upload, and how long a request takes.

blocks.caption: A full estimate: request rates at peak, storage for one year, and the requests in progress at once.

list: Aim for the right order of magnitude, using round numbers.
Requests per second is daily actions divided by about 100,000 seconds, times a peak factor.
Storage is items a day times size times days kept times copies.
Little's law: requests in progress equal the arrival rate times the time per request.
